title: Size-Dependent High-Order Harmonic Generation from Linear Carbon-Chain Molecules in Linearly Polarized Laser Fields
authors: Yifan Kang, Yang Yang, Yingtan Li, Shuwen Pang, Huiwen Yang, Yingdan Zhang, Shushan Zhou
abstract: High-order harmonic generation from molecules is highly sensitive to molecular geometry and strong-field electron dynamics, providing a powerful route for probing and controlling ultrafast processes in extended systems. In this work, we systematically investigate the influence of molecular chain length on HHG from linear carbon-chain molecules C$_2$H$_2$, C$_6$H$_2$, and C$_{10}$H$_2$ driven by an 800 nm linearly polarized laser field. To isolate the molecular-size effect from the influence of different ionization potentials, the laser intensities are adjusted to maintain the same Keldysh parameter for different molecules. Real-time time-dependent density functional theory simulations are performed with the molecular axis aligned parallel to the laser polarization direction. The results show that increasing the molecular chain length significantly enhances the harmonic yield and tends to extend the cutoff region. In particular, C$_{10}$H$_2$ exhibits much stronger plateau harmonics than C$_2$H$_2$, while the intermediate molecule C$_6$H$_2$ shows harmonic intensities between those of C$_2$H$_2$ and C$_{10}$H$_2$. Time-frequency analysis and charge-density evolution reveal that the enhanced HHG emission in longer chains originates from the enlarged electron acceleration distance and increased probability of multi-center recollision, especially near the terminal carbon atoms. These findings demonstrate that molecular-size engineering offers an effective strategy for controlling harmonic emission and optimizing attosecond light sources in extended molecular systems.
summary: This paper uses TDDFT simulations to study High-Order Harmonic Generation (HHG) in linear carbon chains of varying lengths. The key finding is that increasing the molecular size significantly boosts harmonic emission, extending the plateau region. This effect is explained by enhanced electron dynamics, such as increased recollision probability, offering a route for molecular-size engineering of attosecond light sources.
main_problem: The study investigates how the physical size (chain length) of linear carbon molecules affects the efficiency and spectral characteristics of High-Order Harmonic Generation (HHG).
main_result: Increasing the molecular chain length significantly enhances the harmonic yield and extends the cutoff region, which is attributed to increased electron acceleration distance and multi-center recollision.
method: The research employs real-time Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) simulations to model the strong-field electron dynamics.
model_or_system: The system consists of linear carbon-chain molecules ($	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_2$, $	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_2$, $	ext{C}_{10}	ext{H}_2$) aligned parallel to a linearly polarized 800 nm laser field. The simulations are carefully controlled by adjusting laser intensities to maintain a constant Keldysh parameter across different molecules.
key_observables: High-Order Harmonic Generation (HHG) spectra (harmonic yield and cutoff region), time-frequency analysis, and charge-density evolution.
important_parameters: Laser wavelength (800 nm), Keldysh parameter ($\gamma$), and molecular chain length.
main_assumptions: The comparison isolates the molecular-size effect by keeping the Keldysh parameter constant, thereby minimizing the influence of variations in ionization potentials.
figures_summary: Figures compare HHG spectra for different chain lengths ($	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_2$ vs $	ext{C}_{10}	ext{H}_2$), show the size-dependent enhancement, and analyze charge-density evolution revealing enhanced dynamics in longer chains.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the size dependence of HHG, presenting results comparing multiple chain lengths under controlled laser parameters, and interpreting the physical origin of the enhancement via time-domain analysis.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses molecular physics and strong-field quantum optics by demonstrating a controllable, size-dependent mechanism for enhancing attosecond light sources in extended molecular systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. HHG spectra of C2H2 and C10H2 driven by an 800 nm linearly polarized laser field. The molecular axis is parallel to the laser polarization direction, as shown in Fig. 1. The electric-field amplitude is 0.057 a.u. for C10H2 and 0.073 a.u. for C2H2, corresponding to the same Keldysh parameter γ = 0.724. The laser pulse has a trapezoidal envelope with a one-cycle ramp-on, a four-cycle plateau, and a one-cycle ramp-off.

FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of the molecular orientation with respect to the linearly polarized laser field. The molec- ular axes of C2H2, C6H2, and C10H2 are aligned along the z axis, parallel to the laser polarization direction. The molecu- lar lengths are 3.15 a.u., 8.01 a.u., and 12.87 a.u., respectively.

FIG. 3. Time-frequency analysis and charge-density evolution for C2H2 and C10H2. (a,b) HHG spectra and directional components. (c,d) Time-frequency distributions of the HHG spectra, where the dashed lines mark the main harmonic emission times. (e,f) Time-dependent charge variation around representative atomic centers. The stronger charge oscillations near the terminal carbon atoms of C10H2 indicate enhanced electron localization and multi-center recollision in the longer molecule.

FIG. 4. HHG spectra of C2H2 and C10H2 under linearly polarized laser fields with different intensities. For each panel, the laser amplitudes are chosen to maintain the same Keldysh parameter for the two molecules. The results show that the harmonic yield of C10H2 becomes increasingly stronger than that of C2H2 as the field strength increases.

FIG. 5. (a) Comparison of HHG spectra from C2H2, C6H2, and C10H2 under the same Keldysh parameter. (b) Time- frequency analysis of HHG from C6H2, where the dashed line marks the main harmonic emission time. (c) Time-dependent charge variation around representative atomic centers in C6H2 near the main emission time. The results show that the harmonic yield increases with molecular chain length and that terminal carbon atoms contribute strongly to the enhanced emission.
